result: The study successfully employed TurboID proximity labeling in C. elegans to biotinylate proteins near P granule components. CRISPR/Cas9 was used to tag P granule proteins (DEPS-1, GLH-1, IFE-1, PGL-1) with TurboID. Tagged strains showed varying fertility (DEPS-1::TurboID ~88 progeny, TurboID::GLH-1 ~167 progeny, TurboID::IFE-1 ~77 progeny, PGL-1::TurboID sterile), with PGL-1::TurboID toxicity noted. Biotinylation was confirmed by streptavidin-HRP blotting and immunofluorescence, showing enrichment at perinuclear structures.
evaluation: Claims C5-C61 collectively demonstrate successful implementation of TurboID proximity labeling in C. elegans. The methodology is well-documented with CRISPR/Cas9 tagging (C50), fertility assessments (C51-C55), and biotinylation validation through multiple assays (C59-C60). The observation of PGL-1::TurboID toxicity (C54-C56) is appropriately noted as a limitation. P granule marker localization in tagged strains (C57-C58) confirms proper assembly.

result: Mass spectrometry analysis of biotinylated proteins identified 155 proteins enriched by TurboID::GLH-1 and 127 by DEPS-1::TurboID (fold change ≥8, p<0.05), with 78 proteins common to both. The method recovered 90% (18/20) of known P granule proteins and all Z granule proteins (ZNFX-1, WAGO-4), but no Mutator foci proteins (0/11), consistent with P granules physically contacting Z granules but not Mutator foci. Known P granule components (PGL-1, PGL-3, GLH-1-4, Argonaute proteins, RNA metabolism factors) and nuclear pore proteins (NPP-6, NPP-9, NPP-14) were enriched.
evaluation: Claims C62-C77 present comprehensive proteomic data with appropriate statistical thresholds (fold change ≥8, p<0.05). The high recovery rate of known P granule proteins (90%) and selective enrichment of Z granule but not Mutator foci proteins validates the method's specificity. The enrichment of nuclear pore components (C76) is consistent with P granules' perinuclear localization. The absence of nuclear Argonaute HRDE-1 (C73) further supports specificity.

result: Gene ontology analysis of enriched proteins showed top cellular component terms were 'cytoplasmic ribonucleoprotein granule,' 'ribonucleoprotein granule,' and 'P granule.' Biological process terms included 'negative regulation of gene expression,' 'gene silencing by RNA,' and 'posttranscriptional regulation of gene expression.' Molecular function terms included 'RNA binding,' 'nucleic acid binding,' and 'helicase activity.' Protein interaction network analysis of 78 proteins showed 200 edges (p<1×10⁻¹⁶), significantly more than expected by chance. The P granule proteome displayed higher disorder than random controls, suggesting IDR-containing proteins are overrepresented.
evaluation: Claims C78-C87 present bioinformatic analyses that are well-supported by the data. GO enrichment analysis (C78-C81) appropriately identifies P granule-related terms and RNA metabolism functions. The protein interaction network analysis (C83-C85) uses appropriate statistical testing (p<1×10⁻¹⁶) to demonstrate biological connectivity. The disorder analysis (C86-C87) employs IUPred algorithm with proper controls, supporting the conclusion about IDR enrichment.

result: An RNAi screen of 31 candidate genes identified 11 genes whose depletion caused PGL-1::TagRFP phenotypes, including previously known factors (cpf-2, cey-2, cey-3) and novel factor C38D4.4/eggd-1. Depletion of C38D4.4 resulted in large PGL-1 aggregates separated from nuclear envelopes. F58G11.3 (33.3% identical to EGGD-1) was identified from TurboID experiments and named eggd-2, though its RNAi depletion showed no obvious PGL-1 phenotype. These proteins are also referred to as MIP-1 and MIP-2 in an independent study.
evaluation: Claims C8 and C88-C98 describe a functional RNAi screen that successfully identified EGGD-1/EGGD-2 as P granule assembly factors. The screen design is appropriate (31 candidates from proteomic data), and validation of known factors (C89-C90) supports the approach. The identification of EGGD-1 phenotype (C91) is well-documented with microscopy. The lack of eggd-2 RNAi phenotype (C97) is honestly reported and later explained by genetic redundancy.

result: Loss of eggd-1 and eggd-2 causes P granule detachment from nuclear envelope, germline atrophy, and reduced fertility. In eggd-1 mutants, PGL-1::TagRFP dispersed into cytoplasm with increased rachis/edge ratio. eggd-2 single mutants showed minor effects, but eggd-1; eggd-2 double mutants showed severe phenotypes with large cytoplasmic aggregates. In embryos, both proteins are required for P granule partitioning and perinuclear attachment. Fertility was reduced in single mutants (eggd-1: ~170, eggd-2: ~204 progeny vs. wild-type ~263) and severely reduced in double mutants (~37 progeny). Germline mortality assays showed progressive sterility over generations, most rapid in double mutants.
evaluation: Claims C10-C12 and C99-C118 present comprehensive genetic characterization with multiple complementary assays. Microscopy data (C99-C107) demonstrates P granule mislocalization with appropriate quantification (C104-C105). Fertility assays (C111-C115) show clear additive effects in double mutants. Germline mortality assays (C116-C117) provide additional evidence for essential function. The data consistently support partial redundancy between EGGD-1 and EGGD-2, with EGGD-1 playing a more dominant role in adult germline.

result: EGGD-1 and EGGD-2 are putative LOTUS-domain proteins containing two IDRs (one N-terminal, one C-terminal) and two eLOTUS domains, as predicted by HHpred and IUPred algorithms. Both EGGD-1::GFP and mCherry::EGGD-2 are expressed in adult germline and embryonic germ lineage, localizing to perinuclear P granules. EGGD-2 fluorescent signal was much weaker than EGGD-1::GFP. Super-resolution imaging showed EGGD-1::GFP partly co-localizes with PGL-1::TagRFP, enriched at the base of P granules.
evaluation: Claims C9, C119-C125, and C164 characterize EGGD-1/EGGD-2 domain structure and localization using appropriate computational (HHpred, IUPred) and experimental (fluorescent tagging, microscopy) methods. The identification of two eLOTUS domains (C164) is supported by sequence analysis. Localization data (C121-C125) from endogenously tagged proteins provides strong evidence for P granule association. The weaker EGGD-2 signal (C123) is noted but doesn't undermine the conclusion.

result: Domain deletion analysis revealed distinct roles for EGGD-1 domains: IDRs are required to anchor EGGD-1 to nuclear periphery, while LOTUS domains are required for perinuclear P granule localization. Deletion of individual LOTUS domains (ΔLOTUS1 or ΔLOTUS2) caused PGL-1 mislocalization while EGGD-1 remained perinuclear. Deletion of both LOTUS domains caused complete PGL-1 cytoplasmic dispersal. Deletion of individual IDRs partially affected EGGD-1 localization, but deletion of both IDRs (ΔIDR1&2) caused complete EGGD-1 cytoplasmic dispersal and PGL-1 mislocalization.
evaluation: Claims C13-C14 and C126-C132 present systematic domain deletion analysis using CRISPR-generated alleles. The experimental design appropriately tests individual and combined domain deletions. Microscopy observations (C126-C131) clearly demonstrate differential effects of LOTUS vs. IDR deletions on EGGD-1 and PGL-1 localization. The conclusion (C132) that IDRs anchor EGGD-1 while LOTUS domains recruit P granule proteins is well-supported by the deletion phenotypes.

result: Epistasis analysis showed that perinuclear GFP::GLH-1 localization depends primarily on EGGD-1. In eggd-1 mutants, GFP::GLH-1 became diffuse and cytoplasmic, while eggd-2 deletion had no effect. Double mutants showed complete GLH-1 cytoplasmic dispersal. Conversely, RNAi depletion of GLH proteins caused PGL-1::TagRFP cytoplasmic dispersal but EGGD-1::GFP remained perinuclear. Depletion of nuclear pore protein npp-10 caused both PGL-1 and EGGD-1 detachment from nuclear membrane, demonstrating that perinuclear EGGD-1 requires intact nuclear pores and GLH-1 recruitment depends on EGGD-1.
evaluation: Claims C133-C143 present well-designed epistasis experiments using genetic mutants and RNAi to establish the hierarchical relationship: nuclear pores → EGGD-1 → GLH-1 → PGL-1. The bidirectional experiments (testing EGGD effects on GLH-1, and GLH effects on EGGD-1) strengthen the conclusions. The npp-10 RNAi experiments (C140-C141) appropriately test the role of nuclear pores. The logic is sound and conclusions are well-supported.

result: Ectopic expression experiments in muscle cells showed that mCherry::GLH-1 alone was diffuse throughout cytoplasm, while EGGD-1::GFP self-aggregated into granules, with majority associating with nuclear periphery. When both proteins were co-expressed, they co-localized and formed perinuclear foci, demonstrating that EGGD-1 is intrinsically capable of forming perinuclear granules and drives perinuclear granule formation by recruiting GLH-1.
evaluation: Claims C144-C149 present elegant ectopic expression experiments that test sufficiency. The experimental design appropriately uses muscle cells to test protein behavior outside normal germline context. Results clearly show EGGD-1 self-assembly capability (C145-C146) and ability to recruit GLH-1 (C147), supporting the conclusion that EGGD-1 is both necessary and sufficient for perinuclear granule formation. This complements the loss-of-function studies.

result: Background information on germ granules and P granules, including their nomenclature across species, conserved protein components (Piwi proteins, Vasa proteins, LOTUS-domain proteins), and known P granule assembly pathway involving DEPS-1, GLH-1, PGL-1, and IFE-1. P granules are membraneless RNA-rich organelles present throughout C. elegans life cycle with dynamic localization patterns, and cannot be easily purified by conventional fractionation approaches.
evaluation: Claims C1-C47 provide established background knowledge about germ granules and P granules, appropriately cited from literature. These claims establish the scientific context and rationale for the study. The information about P granule composition being elusive (C4) and difficulty of conventional purification (C47) justifies the proximity labeling approach. All claims are well-supported by citations to primary literature.

result: Discussion of P granule assembly mechanisms and EGGD-1/EGGD-2 function. Previous studies showed P granule formation requires PGL-1, PGL-3, GLH-1, GLH-4, MEG-3, and MEG-4. Both this study and Cipriani et al. (2021) show LOTUS-domain proteins are required for C. elegans germline development. A model is proposed where EGGD IDRs interact with nuclear pore cytoplasmic filaments, LOTUS domains bind GLH-1, initiating recruitment of PGL-1 and other P granule proteins. EGGD-1 and EGGD-2 function partially redundantly in adult germline, with EGGD-1 more dominant, but both required in embryos.
evaluation: Claims C150-C162 appropriately discuss findings in context of prior work and propose mechanistic models. The comparison with Cipriani et al. (2021) is appropriate (C152-C153). The proposed model (C155-C158) is clearly labeled as speculative and is reasonable based on the experimental data. The discussion of EGGD-1/EGGD-2 redundancy (C159-C162) is well-supported by the genetic data, though the hypothesis about different Vasa protein interactions (C162) is appropriately speculative.

result: Discussion of LOTUS domain protein family characteristics and evolution. Most LOTUS proteins (Oskar, TDRD5, TDRD7) have single eLOTUS domains, while EGGD-1/EGGD-2 have two. LOTUS domains show minimal sequence homology but adopt common helix-turn-helix conformation and conserved function of binding Vasa. LOTUS proteins are essential for germ cell development across metazoans (Drosophila Oskar, mouse TDRD7, C. elegans EGGD-1/EGGD-2). A third C. elegans LOTUS protein LOTR-1 was also enriched in TurboID experiments. LOTUS domain proteins belong to a unique family with low sequence identity but high structural and functional similarity.
evaluation: Claims C163-C179 provide comparative analysis of LOTUS domain proteins across species, appropriately citing literature. The observation that EGGD-1/EGGD-2 have two eLOTUS domains (C164) is supported by computational analysis. The discussion of LOTUS domain structure-function relationships (C171-C174) is well-supported by citations. The identification of LOTR-1 in TurboID data (C170) provides additional validation. The conclusion about LOTUS protein family characteristics (C179) is reasonable.

result: Discussion of proximity labeling methodology advantages and limitations. TurboID is advantageous for capturing weak/transient interactions and reducing background contaminants, making it ideal for phase-separated organelles. TurboID is optimal for C. elegans due to temperature compatibility, substrate availability, and efficiency. Limitations include potential toxicity and labeling of cytoplasmic proteins. Suggestions for improvement include auxin-inducible degradation systems and split-TurboID methods. The approach could be applied to other germ granules (Z granules, Mutator foci).
evaluation: Claims C180-C197 provide balanced discussion of methodology with appropriate citations. The advantages of proximity labeling (C180-C183) are well-established. The rationale for choosing TurboID (C184-C186) is sound and well-cited. Limitations (C187-C190) are honestly discussed with data support (e.g., C188 references Figure 1D). Suggestions for improvement (C191-C193) are reasonable and appropriately speculative. The proposal to apply the method to other granules (C194-C197) is logical.
